layers.name: User
layers.question: Who needs the compute?
layers.definition: Researchers, students, start-ups, agency analysts who run compute jobs on the network

layers.name: Home institution
layers.question: Who vouches for them and passes along their share?
layers.definition: Universities, colleges, companies or labs that make the user eligible and often sub-allocate a share

layers.name: Allocation
layers.question: Who decides who gets time, and on what basis?
layers.definition: Body of rules that decide access via adjudging the merit of the user's request, institutional quota, purchases, fees or subsidy committees

layers.name: Funding
layers.question: Who pays for hardware and upkeep?
layers.definition: Federal agencies, states, universities, philanthropy, vendors in kind, or user fees.

layers.name: Governance
layers.question: Who sets the rules and can change them?
layers.definition: A board, funding agency, ministry, trustees or advisory body with decision or advice rights.

layers.name: Ownership
layers.question: Who holds title to the hardware?
layers.definition: The legal owner of the compute equipment.

layers.name: Operations
layers.question: Who runs it day to day?
layers.definition: The staff who run the scheduler, systems, security and user support.

layers.name: Facility
layers.question: Whose building, power and cooling?
layers.definition: The data center that houses the equipment and supplies power and cooling.

layers.name: Suppliers
layers.question: Who supplies the hardware and software?
layers.definition: Chip makers, system builders, storage vendors and integrators.

approaches.name: Empire AI
approaches.kind: Independent state-seeded nonprofit, hosted on a public campus
approaches.recency: Beta (a $40M NVIDIA system) came fully online on 5 Aug 2026; allocation enforcement began 1 Sep 2026. The permanent Gamma facility at UB is reported to finish in Jan 2028.
approaches.moneyFlow: More than $500M in public and private money, including up to $340M in state capital through Empire State Development, $25M over ten years in SUNY operating funds and $50M in private matching funds from three new members. Each member institution receives 700,000 [[service unit]]s a year and splits them internally.
approaches.summary: The state supplies most of the capital. Its agency NYSTAR sits on the board as an observer, while public universities (SUNY, CUNY, UB) and NY CREATES, a nonprofit set up by Empire State Development and SUNY, hold director seats alongside private members. Compute is divided equally among member institutions.

approaches.name: MGHPCC and AICR
approaches.kind: Member-owned facility with a state-funded AI layer and a public set-aside
approaches.recency: Vendors were selected on 12 Dec 2025 (Cambridge Computer with Dell and VAST). Documentation is live and the first users were onboarding in 2026.
approaches.moneyFlow: A $31M MassTech grant plus member matching, which the state puts at about $120M over five years. Member universities fund operations. At least 40% of compute time is reserved for startups, non-member colleges and nonprofits.
approaches.summary: Six universities own and govern a shared data center nonprofit. The state bought a GPU cluster inside it in exchange for a [[set-aside]] of compute for outside users. The state's lever is the grant contract, not a board seat.

approaches.name: Ohio Supercomputer Center
approaches.kind: State-funded service run by a state university
approaches.recency: The 2025–26 Research Report cites 7,715 clients. FY26 prices were unchanged. The center has operated since 1987.
approaches.moneyFlow: State operating funds (line item GRF 235510, about $5.1M a year) through the Ohio Department of Higher Education, administered by Ohio State as fiscal agent, plus subsidized fees. Each Ohio academic PI gets a $1,000 annual credit; classroom use is fully subsidized; commercial clients pay.
approaches.summary: OSC is a division of the state's higher education department, but Ohio State's Office of the CIO operates it for the state and acts as fiscal agent. Any Ohio institution can use it without membership dues, and a statewide users group advises.

approaches.name: TACC Horizon
approaches.kind: Funder-owned national facility, run by one lead campus
approaches.recency: Horizon's GPU phase entered early operations in Jul 2026, with early users from late summer 2026. The CPU phase is expected in winter 2026 or early 2027.
approaches.moneyFlow: NSF's $457M [[MREFC]] construction investment, with operations planned over decades. Allocations are free and decided by [[merit review]].
approaches.summary: The national funder sets the mission and the allocation rules. One university builds and runs the system, which sits in a commercial [[colocation]] data center.

approaches.name: SDSC Expanse2
approaches.kind: Variant: a UC campus unit running a national system
approaches.recency: NSF awarded $10M for Expanse2 in Sep 2026 to replace Expanse. SDSC also leads the NAIRR Operations Center from 1 Sep 2026.
approaches.moneyFlow: A $10M NSF acquisition award. SDSC is an [[organized research unit]] of UC San Diego, reported in 2021 to manage a budget above $50M.
approaches.summary: A University of California campus unit houses and runs a national system in its own data center, with national allocation policies.

approaches.name: NCSA DeltaAI
approaches.kind: Variant: national system with set-asides for the host campus and state
approaches.recency: DeltaAI is in production. R. Srikant became NCSA director on 1 Jan 2026.
approaches.moneyFlow: NSF grants of nearly $30M, additional State of Illinois funding, and 20 extra nodes from Illinois Computes, a $30M campus program. Illinois researchers receive 10% of the NSF-funded allocation.
approaches.summary: Most capacity is allocated nationally through ACCESS, with shares for the NAIRR Pilot, the host campus and state-funded nodes. One system serves three allocation channels.

approaches.name: PSC Bridges-3
approaches.kind: Variant: one center run jointly by two universities
approaches.recency: NSF awarded $10M for Bridges-3 in Jun 2026 and $5M for a hybrid quantum-classical system in Jul 2026.
approaches.moneyFlow: Federal grants, with Carnegie Mellon as the award recipient, plus Commonwealth line items. The latest verified state amount is $500K in FY2020–21 plus $1M in capital.
approaches.summary: Carnegie Mellon and the University of Pittsburgh run the center together. When the director left in 2022, the two universities named interim co-directors and a joint search committee.

approaches.name: NAIRR and ACCESS
approaches.location: National (led from San Diego with Austin)
approaches.recency: The NAIRR Operations Center was established on 1 Sep 2026. The pilot supported more than 800 projects with more than 25 private partners. The ACCESS Variable Marketplace launched in Jun 2026.
approaches.moneyFlow: A $35M cooperative award over five years to SDSC (one outlet reported three years). Hardware is paid for separately by [[resource provider]]s and partners. Users receive free, merit-reviewed credits redeemable across providers.
approaches.summary: The layer owns no hardware. It governs access across many providers through a portal, review and exchangeable credits.

approaches.name: RMACC and Alpine
approaches.kind: Variant: a regional consortium using one host's cluster
approaches.recency: The 2025–26 board is seated. Alpine is the shared system.
approaches.moneyFlow: Alpine is jointly funded by CU Boulder, CU Anschutz, Colorado State and NSF (award 2201538). Access is free to member researchers under [[fair-share scheduling]].
approaches.summary: A regional collaborative housed at CU Boulder owns no hardware. Smaller member institutions reach a host university's cluster at no charge.

approaches.name: DOE Genesis Mission
approaches.kind: Federal science platform on national-lab computing
approaches.recency: Genesis Mission launched by Executive Order 14363 in Nov 2025; 278 projects selected on 22 Jul 2026; 12 Phase II awards ($159M) in Oct 2026. Separately, DOE selected four federal sites for privately financed AI data centers (Jul 2025); they are not included here because no public access has been announced.
approaches.moneyFlow: DOE funds selected projects; cloud providers donate credits, for example Crusoe ($50M) and Microsoft ($40M in Azure credits).
approaches.summary: DOE turns its national-lab supercomputers, secure cloud, data and models into one platform for selected research teams. Compute is publicly owned at the labs or donated by cloud providers.

approaches.name: HiPerGator
approaches.recency: The fourth-generation system was planned for production by Sep 2025, with 504 B200 GPUs. It has nearly 7,000 users.
approaches.moneyFlow: A $70M partnership in 2020 ($25M from alumnus Chris Malachowsky, $25M in NVIDIA in kind, $20M from UF) and a $24M upgrade approved in Dec 2024. Users buy compute units at subsidized rates under an [[investment model]].
approaches.summary: One university owns, hosts and runs the cluster. Access follows purchase, and UF's trustees opened purchase to every Florida institution on UF's terms.

approaches.name: Purdue RCAC
approaches.kind: Variant: community clusters beside a national system
approaches.recency: Gautschi is in production; the Bell cluster retires on 31 Oct 2026.
approaches.moneyFlow: Faculty buy into community clusters; Purdue Computes funded Gautschi. Anvil was funded by a $10M NSF award and is allocated through ACCESS.
approaches.summary: One operator runs two tracks: clusters that Purdue groups buy into, and a national system whose access is decided elsewhere.

approaches.name: CSCS and Alps
approaches.kind: National resource placed inside one university
approaches.recency: The 2026 fact sheet is current. The Swiss AI Initiative's third call ran to 31 Mar 2026, with projects starting in Jul 2026.
approaches.moneyFlow: The Swiss Confederation funds CSCS through the ETH Board and ETH Zurich. Compute is free through the User Lab. The Swiss AI Initiative was seeded with more than 10M GPU hours and a CHF 20M grant.
approaches.summary: An autonomous unit of one university carries a national mandate. Independent experts review proposals, and another university moved its own computing service into CSCS.

approaches.name: Gauss Centre
approaches.kind: Association of three centers with federal–state cost sharing
approaches.recency: The 36th large-scale call (Jul 2026) allocates time for Nov 2026 to Oct 2027.
approaches.moneyFlow: Hunter and SuperMUC-NG are funded half by the federal research ministry and half by their host states. JUPITER is funded 50% by EuroHPC, 25% federally and 25% by North Rhine-Westphalia.
approaches.summary: A [[registered association]] links three centers that stay inside their parent institutions. Researchers apply through joint, peer-reviewed calls.

approaches.name: ABCI 3.0
approaches.kind: Government lab owns, its company runs
approaches.recency: Because demand exceeded projections, point issuance closed on 30 Sep 2025, mostly due to public-sector use. FY2026 status is not verified.
approaches.moneyFlow: METI [[supplementary budget]]s fund the system. Users prepay for points (220 yen per point in FY2024), with a cheaper tier for universities, public bodies and nonprofits.
approaches.summary: A national research institute built the system and its commercial subsidiary operates it. When capacity ran out, users were pointed to domestic commercial clouds.

approaches.name: IndiaAI compute portal
approaches.recency: Figures given to Parliament in Aug 2026 show 93.18 lakh (about 9.3 million) GPU hours sanctioned across 237 projects, with 15 empanelled providers.
approaches.moneyFlow: A five-year outlay of Rs 10,371.92 crore. Eligible users pay a subsidized rate of about Rs 100 per GPU-hour against a market rate of $2.50–3.
approaches.summary: A ministry division subsidizes access to GPUs owned by private providers chosen through public empanelment. The public side owns no hardware.

approaches.name: CENIC AIR
approaches.kind: Member-contributed platform on the state research network
approaches.recency: Introduced at CENIC's 2024 conference; CSU campuses joining.
approaches.moneyFlow: NSF grants support the national platform; campuses buy and contribute their own hardware. No state appropriation found.
approaches.summary: Campuses contribute GPUs and storage to a shared national platform and their faculty use it without merit review. SDSC and CENIC built the California portion; the platform is governed by its member institutions.

categories.name: Users
categories.wants: Fast, predictable access to enough compute for the work.
categories.paysOrRisks: Proposal writing, wait times, fees beyond free allowances.
categories.lever: Choose where to run work; their demand justifies funding.

categories.name: Home institutions
categories.wants: Research standing, faculty recruitment and student training.
categories.paysOrRisks: Buy-in money, staff time, internal disputes over how to split a share.
categories.lever: Pass a share along or hold it back; vouch for eligibility.

categories.name: State and national governments
categories.wants: Economic development, talent and public research capacity.
categories.paysOrRisks: Capital and operating money; political exposure if the system sits idle.

categories.name: Federal and supranational funders
categories.wants: National research capacity and fair access across institutions.
categories.paysOrRisks: Oversight effort; fixed-term awards that end on a set date.
categories.lever: Award terms, merit review rules and renewal decisions.

categories.name: Philanthropy
categories.wants: Fast, visible impact for a mission.
categories.paysOrRisks: Gifts and loaned equipment; little say unless granted a seat.
categories.lever: Conditions attached to gifts; observer seats.

categories.name: Industry and vendors
categories.wants: Reference customers, future orders and ecosystem influence.
categories.lever: Supply terms, credits and technical dependence.

categories.name: Operators and staff
categories.paysOrRisks: Staffing costs, upkeep, long refresh cycles.

categories.name: Facility hosts
categories.wants: Rent, a strategic tenant or campus prestige.

The system sits in a commercial colocation data center, not a university building.

journeys.asA: a graduate student at a small college
journeys.iWant: free credits for an AI project
journeys.soThat: I can finish my thesis experiments

steps.caption: The student requests free ACCESS credits.
Credits are redeemed at a provider of their choosing, at provider-set rates.
For an AI project, the student can also apply through the NAIRR portal.
The NAIRR may match the project to a private partner's resources.
NSF funds provider systems through separate awards.

friction.text: Provider-set rates mean the same credits buy different amounts of time at different providers.
Part of the national resource is privately owned capacity contributed by more than 25 partners.
Independent peer reviewers score requests on focus-area alignment, readiness, feasibility, need, team and justification; public benefit is not a named criterion.
Matching committees that pair projects with private resources include the private partners, who can see reviews for their category.

journeys.asA: a lab team on a Genesis project
journeys.soThat: our science workflow runs on schedule

steps.caption: The team submits a Genesis Mission project and is selected.
Selected Phase II teams receive DOE awards.
Work can run on cloud credits donated to the program.

friction.text: Compute arrives as donated credits from cloud providers, whose terms the program does not set alone.

journeys.soThat: we can run AI work without building our own cluster

steps.caption: The faculty member's department arranges a purchase; a three-month trial is free.
The department buys compute and GPU units at UF rates.
UF Research Computing allocates the purchased units to the group.
UF's trustees set equal terms for Florida institutions.

friction.text: Access follows purchase, so groups with more money get more compute.

journeys.context: Swiss university outside the ETH Domain
journeys.asA: a researcher at a cantonal university
journeys.soThat: my team can train a domain model

steps.caption: The researcher submits a User Lab proposal for free time on Alps.
For the Swiss AI large grants, the lead applicant must hold an ETH Domain appointment.
Federal money reaches CSCS through the ETH Board and ETH Zurich.
CSCS runs as an autonomous unit of ETH Zurich.

friction.text: Lead applicants for Swiss AI large grants must come from the ETH Domain.

journeys.soThat: we can run a year of production simulations

steps.caption: The scientist answers a large-scale call, open twice a year with a strict deadline.
Peer reviewers award time on JUPITER at Jülich.
EuroHPC pays half of JUPITER.
The federal ministry and North Rhine-Westphalia each pay a quarter.

friction.text: Calls open twice a year, so a project that misses a deadline waits about six months.

journeys.asA: an engineer in a university lab
journeys.iWant: ABCI points for a training run
journeys.soThat: we can develop a Japanese-language model

steps.caption: The engineer buys points and applies through AIST Solutions.
Jobs run on ABCI 3.0 at the AIST Kashiwa Center.
METI supplementary budgets paid for the system.
AIST's operating company runs the service.

friction.text: Point sales closed early because demand ran past capacity, and users were pointed to commercial clouds.
The system is publicly built but run by a commercial subsidiary.

journeys.asA: a founder of an early-stage startup
journeys.soThat: we can train without paying global cloud rates

steps.caption: The founder applies through the IndiaAI compute portal.
The request is assigned to an empanelled private provider.
The ministry subsidizes the rate.
The startup pays about Rs 100 per GPU-hour.

friction.text: Every GPU is privately owned; the public side brokers and subsidizes access.
Reported gaps between announced and deployed GPUs have not been confirmed by the ministry.

journeys.asA: a faculty member at a CSU campus
journeys.iWant: GPU time for a machine-learning course and a small research project
journeys.soThat: my students and I can train models without buying our own hardware

steps.caption: The faculty member signs in with CILogon and creates a project (a Kubernetes namespace).
The scheduler places the work on whatever contributed hardware is free, wherever it sits.
Campuses that want more capacity buy and contribute their own nodes, often with NSF CC* awards.
NSF supports the national platform's staff and services.

friction.text: The platform is run from UC San Diego with CENIC, and CSU campuses join one at a time: five are named users and two more have expressed interest.
No allocation process is described: work runs on whatever contributed hardware is free, so capacity depends on what campuses choose to buy and share.
Hardware stays with the campuses that buy it; the shared platform schedules capacity it does not own.

purposes.name: Safe and ethical AI
purposes.paraphrase: The framework is to advance the development and deployment of AI that is safe and ethical.

purposes.name: Equitable access to compute
purposes.paraphrase: The framework is to enable equitable innovation by expanding access to computational resources.

purposes.name: Public-benefit research
purposes.paraphrase: The framework is to foster research and innovation that benefits the public.

purposes.name: Sustainable AI
purposes.paraphrase: The framework is to advance AI that is sustainable.

purposes.name: Publicly owned and hosted
purposes.paraphrase: CalCompute is to include a fully owned and hosted cloud platform with staff to run it and support users.

purposes.name: Workforce and labor standards
purposes.paraphrase: The consortium operates under relevant labor and workforce laws; the report addresses the public-sector workforce and equitable pathways.

purposes.name: Placement within UC
purposes.paraphrase: The consortium is to make reasonable efforts to establish CalCompute within the University of California, to the extent possible.

glossary.definition: The decision of who gets how much compute, usually counted in hours or units.
An accounting unit for compute time. Empire AI values one service unit at about $0.50.
Proposals judged by expert panels on scientific merit and broader impact.
A federal award in which the funding agency stays substantially involved in the work.
NSF's Major Research Equipment and Facilities Construction account, used for large facilities.
Housing servers in a data center owned by another company.
A scheduler setting that balances use across groups based on their recent use.
A share of capacity reserved for a defined group of users.
Groups buy shares of a cluster and receive access in proportion to what they bought. Also called a condo model.
A center that owns and runs a system offered through a national allocation program.
Approval of private providers to sell into a government program at agreed rates.
An EU legal body that pools EU and member-state money for a shared purpose, such as EuroHPC.
A German nonprofit legal form (eingetragener Verein, e.V.).
A University of California designation for a campus research center.
A mid-year budget in Japan, used to fund ABCI's construction and expansion.
Contributions of goods or services instead of cash.
SB 53's framework element for CalCompute: a cloud platform the public side owns and houses, with staff to run it.

ui.app.name: Compute Governance Explainer
ui.start.title: Start here
ui.start.purpose: This site explains how shared AI and high-performance computing is organized today: who owns the hardware, who hosts and runs it, who pays, who sets the rules and who decides who gets time. It was built to inform the governance section of the CalCompute framework report under California SB 53.
ui.start.stack.title: The stack between a researcher and a GPU
ui.start.stack.intro: Nine layers sit between a person who needs compute and the hardware. One organization can hold one layer, or several of them. The approaches differ mainly in which layers are held together and which are split across stakeholders.
ui.start.read.title: How to read the views
ui.start.read.shapes: Each shape is an organization. A tall shape spanning several layers represents that is one organization handling all said layers.
ui.start.read.flows: Lines show four kinds of flow: requests (solid), money (dashed), control (dotted) and location (double line, where a request crosses into another place).
ui.start.read.status: Every fact carries a status: verified, reported, not public or inferred. Select a fact to see its source. Ownership is the least documented layer: title to equipment is rarely published, so most ownership facts are inferred from who bought the equipment and under which award. Funding facts start with Capital, Operating, In kind or Program.
ui.start.ways.title: Four ways in
ui.start.ways.explore.title: Explore an approach
ui.start.ways.explore.text: Pick one of seventeen configurations and see which stakeholder handles each layer.
ui.start.ways.journeys.title: Follow a journey
ui.start.ways.journeys.text: Trace one user's request down the stack and the related financing in action for the user's successful use.
ui.start.ways.compare.title: Compare up to three layers
ui.start.ways.compare.text: See side by side where the layers are held differently.
ui.start.ways.stakeholders.title: Follow one stakeholder
ui.start.ways.stakeholders.text: See a state government, a funder or a vendor across every approach.
ui.start.approaches.title: Seventeen noted configurations of the stakeholders' ownership across the compute stack
ui.start.approaches.text: Eight U.S. approaches, six variants and four international contrast cases. Select one to open it in Explore.
ui.app.tagline: Who owns, hosts, runs, funds, governs and allocates shared AI compute
ui.notice: An explainer of how shared AI and HPC compute is organized today, built to inform the CalCompute governance framework under California SB 53
ui.explore.title: Explore
ui.explore.intro: Pick an approach, then a view. Drag to turn, scroll or pinch to zoom, and select a shape for deeper detail.
ui.journeys.title: Journeys
ui.journeys.intro: One user story per approach. Follow a user's compute request down the stack and the money that finances it flow across the chain, and see where friction meets SB 53's purposes. Personas are illustrative.
ui.compare.title: Compare approaches
ui.compare.intro: Choose up to three. Tall blocks are one organization holding several layers. Shaded layer names mark rows where the holders differ.
ui.stakeholders.title: Stakeholders
ui.stakeholders.intro: Pick a stakeholder category to see what it wants, what it risks, what lever it holds, and where it sits in every approach.
ui.spectrum.title: Bundling spectrum
ui.spectrum.intro: Each approach compared by the number of organizations holding layers 2 to 8. Select one to open it in the explorer.

changelog.change: Added CENIC AIR as a California case. Narrowed DOE to the Genesis Mission and removed the federal-land data center sites, which offer no public access. Corrected governance for Empire AI, OSC and NCSA. Separated labels about funding under 'capital' or 'operating'. Added friction points for public-benefit research, sustainability, workforce and UC placement, and a note on how statuses are assigned. Added the CalCompute logo and browser icon.
Standardized Title across README, Master .xlsx and web UI
Added traffic counter and web analytics via goatcounter
Cleaned language, corrected phrasing issues, removed open_questions tab
Added a Start here page and organization logos throughout. Group entries show the logos of named members.
First release on real data: 16 configurations (7 approaches, 5 variants, 4 contrast cases), 11 journeys tagged to SB 53 purposes, Strata and Constellation views.
Prototype with filler data to settle the interface.
